Healthcare Professionals Report Favourable Artificial Intelligence Attitudes Despite Specific Anxiety Patterns

A systematic review of 44 cross-sectional studies has found that healthcare professionals and healthcare students generally express favourable attitudes toward artificial intelligence, although specific perspectives vary across diverse populations and measurement instruments. Synthesising evidence from 28,452 participants across 19 countries, the authors observed widespread positive reception toward clinical technological advancement alongside identifiable, non-generalised patterns of artificial intelligence anxiety documented specifically within Turkish study cohorts.

Conducted in strict accordance with PRISMA 2020 guidelines and registered prospectively with PROSPERO under registration code CRD420261286794, the systematic review aimed to synthesise available evidence regarding attitudes and anxiety toward artificial intelligence among healthcare professionals and healthcare students. Two authors independently carried out the literature searches across five electronic databases, specifically PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane Library, CINAHL, and Embase, utilising targeted combinations of Medical Subject Headings and text keywords for artificial intelligence, the target population, and attitude or anxiety outcomes. The search identified descriptive, cross-sectional, or observational research articles published between 1 January 2016 and 31 January 2026, and methodological quality was systematically evaluated using the Joanna Briggs Institute critical appraisal checklist for analytical cross-sectional studies.

From 146 initial records identified across the five electronic databases, 44 cross-sectional studies representing a total of 28,452 participants met the formal inclusion criteria. Individual study sample sizes ranged from 107 to 4,492 participants across 19 countries, originating predominantly from Türkiye and Middle Eastern nations. In terms of outcome distribution across the included literature, 36 studies assessed participant attitudes toward artificial intelligence exclusively, seven investigated artificial intelligence anxiety as their sole outcome, and one single study assessed both attitude and anxiety simultaneously.

Many reviewed studies reported favourable attitudes toward artificial intelligence, though findings varied across distinct surveyed groups and measurement instruments. Demographic analysis revealed that male gender was associated with more favourable attitudes in five studies, whereas one study reported the opposite outcome showing less favourable attitudes among men. Prior artificial intelligence training or knowledge was linked to more favourable attitudes or lower anxiety in only a modest subset of studies, while evaluations examining age and professional seniority produced mixed and inconclusive results.

Artificial intelligence anxiety was evidenced exclusively in Turkish participant samples, where emotional reactions followed identifiable patterns rather than representing a generalised or non-specific fear. Within these Turkish cohorts, artificial intelligence anxiety showed associations in some studies with participant age, gender, prior training, and existing knowledge regarding artificial intelligence technologies. Because the underlying research rested entirely upon cross-sectional observational designs, the authors noted that these findings demonstrate statistical associations rather than direct causal effects.

Methodological appraisal revealed important limitations in the existing evidence base, notably that most attitude studies relied upon self-developed survey instruments rather than validated measurement tools. Consequently, the authors concluded that the synthesized data is best interpreted as a qualitative narrative summary rather than a pooled quantitative estimate. Future quantitative synthesis will require comparable, validated instruments to systematically evaluate attitudes and anxiety toward artificial intelligence across healthcare disciplines.

Subject of Research: Attitudes and anxiety toward healthcare artificial intelligence among clinicians and students

Article Title: Attitudes and anxiety toward artificial intelligence among healthcare professionals and students: a systematic review

Article References: Prerna, Yadav, R., & Jelly, P. (2026). Attitudes and anxiety toward artificial intelligence among healthcare professionals and students: a systematic review. BMC Nursing. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12912-026-05534-7

Keywords: artificial intelligence, healthcare professionals, healthcare students, systematic review, AI anxiety, PRISMA 2020, PROSPERO, cross-sectional studies, JBI critical appraisal, medical technology, attitude measurement, Middle East healthcare, Türkiye healthcare, AI training, clinical education, observational research

News Source: Glenn Wilkins. (November 27, 2026). Healthcare Professionals Report Favourable Artificial Intelligence Attitudes Despite Specific Anxiety Patterns. Scienmag.
